title: Double hamburger on white bun, 2 medium patties

content.title: About
content.content: The double hamburger consists of two medium beef patties (about 100 g each) placed between a split white bun. It is usually topped with lettuce, tomato slice, pickles, onion, cheese, sauce and seasonings. This classic fast‑food item is popular worldwide.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first double hamburger appeared in the United States in the 1930s as a “two‑in‑one” variant.
White buns typically contain more sugar and fat than whole‑grain buns, giving them a softer, sweeter texture.
A 100 g patty is considered “medium” in the fast‑food industry; two such patties provide roughly 200 g of meat.
The combination of two patties and sauce raises the calorie count to 600–800 kcal depending on toppings.
In some countries the double hamburger is served without cheese to highlight the beef flavor.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Two beef patties deliver about 40 g of protein, essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Iron
items.content: Beef is rich in heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Beef provides vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Zinc
items.content: Zinc from the meat supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Calcium (when cheese is added)
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A double hamburger can contain 600–800 kcal, which may contribute to weight gain if eaten frequently.

items.title: Saturated fat and cholesterol
items.content: Beef and cheese contain saturated fats that, in excess, can raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Sauces and pickles add a significant amount of sodium, which can be problematic for people with hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The white bun is made from wheat, making the product unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked beef patties may harbor pathogenic bacteria such as E. coli.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The burger is typically eaten by hand, holding it by the bun. Additional sauce can be added, the bun can be swapped for a whole‑grain version, or cheese can be omitted to reduce calories.

content.title: Storage
content.content: A prepared burger can be stored in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze it and reheat in an oven or microwave before serving.
